children.label: Mapping the Local Group of Galaxies

children.value: Context
In this practice, we are going to make a map of the
Local Group

of galaxies (and associated star clusters).  Roughly speaking, the Local Group refers to the gravitationally-bound group of galaxies within which the Milky Way resides; it spans out to roughly 10 million light years from the Milky Way (3 Megaparsecs, in more common units in the field). This volume contains just two massive galaxies -- the Milky Way and Andromeda -- in addition to hundreds of low mass dwarf galaxies and thousands of star clusters as well.
We usually think of the positions of things in the Local Group in
Supergalactic

Cartesian coordinates (X, Y, Z); however, we cannot observe these directly. Instead, we typically record the angular positions of stars/galaxies etc in “Right Ascension” (0-360 degrees) and “Declination” (-90 to 90 degrees) as well as their distances with respect to the Sun (their “heliocentric distances”); these measurable quantities can be converted so long as one assumes a coordinate frame for the Local Group.
For today’s exercise, we’re going to give you this conversion in the form of a function below.

from astropy import units as u
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
import numpy as np

def convert_to_supergalactic(ra, dec, distance_kpc):
    """
    Convert RA, Dec, and heliocentric distance to Supergalactic Coordinates.
    
    Parameters:
        ra (float): Right Ascension in degrees
        dec (float): Declination in degrees
        distance (float): Heliocentric distance in kpc
        
    Returns:
        tuple: (SGX, SGY, SGZ) in Mpc
    """
    # Create a SkyCoord object
    coord = SkyCoord(ra=ra * u.deg, dec=dec * u.deg, distance=distance * u.kpc, frame='icrs')
    
    # Convert to Supergalactic coordinates
    sg_coord = coord.transform_to('supergalactic')
    
    # Convert to Cartesian coordinates
    sgx = sg_coord.cartesian.x.to(u.Mpc).value
    sgy = sg_coord.cartesian.y.to(u.Mpc).value
    sgz = sg_coord.cartesian.z.to(u.Mpc).value
    
    return sgx, sgy, sgz
An example of using this function for a single trio of (RA,DEC,distance):

# Example usage:
ra = 180.0  # degrees
dec = 45.0  # degrees
distance = 10.0  # kpc
sgx, sgy, sgz = convert_to_supergalactic(ra, dec, distance)
print(f"SGX: {sgx:.2f} kpc")
print(f"SGY: {sgy:.2f} kpc")
print(f"SGZ: {sgz:.2f} kpc")
